The same average return can compound into different wealth: read the growth factors

Compare paired annual returns, signed gains and losses, capital paths and sensitivity scenarios while holding the arithmetic mean and initial investment constant.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore the same arithmetic mean with different paired return spreads

Interactive planning lab

Arithmetic mean of the chosen annual returns5.00%
Annual compound rate of every complete two-year pair3.08%
Smooth-path ending value minus alternating-path ending value$8,197.62

Original deterministic return illustration, with one initial amount and no external deposits or withdrawals. Every complete pair contains mean plus spread and mean minus spread; the arithmetic mean is therefore held constant. The selected number of pairs always produces an even horizon. Returns are nominal total returns with all distributions retained; no separate dividend yield is added. The smooth comparison earns the mean every year as a mathematical reference, not an available guaranteed return. A reversed pair changes interim balances but has the same complete-pair product without cash flows. No asset prices, historical series, market forecast, probabilities, inflation, fee, tax, contribution schedule or suitable allocation is calculated. Holding an arithmetic mean fixed while changing the spread is a controlled comparison, not a claim about achievable investments.

The central idea

A sequence compounds by multiplying growth factors. Its arithmetic average does not automatically equal the annual rate that reproduces the ending wealth.

01

Define the average before using it in a plan

An arithmetic average adds the individual annual returns and divides by the number of years. A compound annual rate asks a different question: what constant annual growth factor would reproduce the change from beginning capital to ending capital over the whole period?

The default pair is a 25% first-year return followed by a negative 15% second-year return. The arithmetic mean is (25% − 15%) ÷ 2, or 5%. A separate smooth reference earns 5% in each year. These paths have the same arithmetic mean, but their growth factors are different.

The FINRA return-calculation explanation provides general context for annualized performance and compounding. All return paths and amounts here are independently hypothetical, without a historical market series, investment offer or forecast.

02

Multiply one plus each return

Start with CAD 10,000 and no later deposits or withdrawals. A 25% gain multiplies it by 1.25, taking it to CAD 12,500. The following 15% loss multiplies that larger balance by 0.85, leaving CAD 10,625. The two-year total gain is 6.25%.

The smooth 5% reference instead multiplies the same starting amount by 1.05 twice. It ends at CAD 11,025, a 10.25% total gain. Applying the arithmetic mean as a constant compound assumption would therefore overstate this particular alternating path’s ending amount by CAD 400 after one pair.

The signed bars show the chosen gains and losses around zero. Their percentages are annual total returns, with distributions retained. They are not returns on the original dollar amount each time. The loss in the second year acts on the balance that exists after the first year’s gain.

03

Calculate the compound rate of a complete pair

If the arithmetic mean is m and each return differs from it by s, the two factors are 1 + m + s and 1 + m − s. Their product is (1 + m)2 − s2. Rates are decimals inside this expression.

The annual compound rate for that complete two-year pair is therefore square root of [(1 + m)2 − s2] minus one. With m = 0.05 and s = 0.20, the result is approximately 3.08% per year. It reproduces CAD 10,625 after two years from CAD 10,000.

When the spread is zero, both returns equal the mean and the compound rate matches it. Increasing the spread while fixing this arithmetic mean reduces the product in this constructed comparison. That is a mathematical condition of the example, rather than a claim that a real investor can hold expected return unchanged while freely choosing volatility.

04

Separate return spread from return order

The capital chart also reverses the pair, applying negative 15% first and positive 25% second. Its first-year balance is different, but its two-year endpoint is the same: multiplication of the two factors gives the same product in either order.

The model repeats only complete pairs, so the two alternating paths meet every second year and at the selected final date. No later contribution or withdrawal changes the money exposed to either return. The different interim balances still matter to someone who needs to sell early, but such a sale is outside this model.

This distinction helps separate two lessons. Different return spreads can produce different compound growth under the same arithmetic mean. Different order alone does not change a full-period product when the same factors apply to an untouched initial investment. Read the related retirement guide for the separate effect of withdrawals during the path.

05

Read longer horizons and the sensitivity matrix as assumptions

The grouped bars compare two, ten, twenty and thirty years while retaining selected capital, mean and spread. In the default twenty-year case, the smooth reference finishes about CAD 8,197.62 above the repeated alternating pair. This difference is not a fee debited from an account; it is the difference between two modeled ending values.

The matrix changes the arithmetic mean and the percentage-point spread, then displays the annual compound rate of a complete pair. Negative cells identify a compound loss even where an arithmetic mean may be zero or positive. Shading does not assign a likelihood to those return patterns.

Both tools deliberately use deterministic paths. They do not estimate an asset’s expected return, statistical volatility, diversification benefit or probability of reaching a goal. A real portfolio will not generally alternate between two fixed annual returns, and its fees, taxes, cash flows and changing holdings may matter.

06

Keep the growth convention consistent with the cash-flow model

Before entering a return assumption into a financial plan, record whether it is nominal or real, arithmetic or geometric, before or after costs, and based on what period or source. A number without those definitions can be applied in a way that changes its meaning.

A constant-rate savings calculator uses its entered return as a compounding rule. It does not simulate a distribution simply because the label says “average.” Adding contributions or withdrawals requires modeling their dates; the geometric rate of an untouched initial investment is not automatically the household’s money-weighted result.

Use the example as a check on interpretation, not a reason to assume a guaranteed smooth return or select a particular investment. For a real goal, also examine the time the money can remain invested, the effect of an early loss, costs, taxes and flexible funding choices. The purpose of the graphs is to make the rate definition and multiplication visible before a single average is allowed to stand in for the entire plan.
